course.title: Calculus II: Series and Differential Equations
course.description: New functions and techniques, infinite series from geometric sums to Taylor polynomials, and differential equations from cooling coffee to oscillators.
course.audience: A capable adult who has met limits, derivatives of powers, the chain rule, antiderivatives and areas in Discere's calculus course. Exponentials, logarithms, sines, the product rule, substitution and parts are covered here, since the first course stops before them.

paragraphs: A balance earning interest grows at a rate that depends on how much it already holds, and a cup of coffee cools more slowly as it approaches room temperature. In each case the quantity is a function of time whose rate of change is tied to its own value, and an equation of that kind is called a differential equation. The simplest is solved by the exponential function, whose derivative is a constant multiple of itself, and the others have solutions that level off at a ceiling or swing back and forth like a sine wave.

A function that is hard to compute can often be written as a sum that never ends, called an infinite series. Whether such a sum has a total depends on how quickly its terms shrink: 1 + ½ + ¼ + … comes to exactly 2, while 1 + ½ + ⅓ + … grows without limit even though its terms also tend to 0. When a sum of powers of x does settle, as e^x = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6 + … does for every x, it turns the function into arithmetic that a machine can carry out, and an error bound says how many terms a given accuracy needs.

Taken together, series and differential equations let calculus go beyond the functions that have tidy formulas. A rule for how a quantity changes can be turned into the quantity itself, exactly when the equation can be solved and step by step when it cannot, and an integral with no antiderivative can still be evaluated to any accuracy by summing a series, with a bound on how far the answer can be from the truth.
outcomes: You'll be able to differentiate and integrate exponentials, logarithms, sines and cosines, using the product rule, substitution and parts.
You'll be able to sum a geometric series and choose a test to decide whether a series converges.
You'll be able to bound the error of an alternating series and of a Taylor polynomial.
You'll be able to find a power series's radius of convergence and use series to evaluate an integral.
You'll be able to solve exponential, separable and logistic equations, step any first-order equation with Euler's method and solve a linear oscillator.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Calculus: Change and Accumulation, Maths Foundations and Trigonometry.

modules.title: More functions to work with
modules.description: Exponentials, products, substitution, parts and waves: the functions and techniques series and differential equations need.

modules.title: Infinite sums
modules.description: When adding forever settles, how to test it, and how functions become power series.

modules.title: Differential equations
modules.description: Rates that depend on the state: models, exact solutions, stepping by hand and in code, and oscillators.

concepts.title: Derivative of e^x
concepts.summary: d/dx e^x = e^x; with the chain rule, d/dx e^(kx) = k e^(kx).

concepts.title: Natural logarithm
concepts.summary: ln x undoes e^x and d/dx ln x = 1/x; d/dx a^x = a^x ln a.

concepts.title: Product rule
concepts.summary: (u v)' = u' v + u v'.

concepts.title: Substitution
concepts.summary: Replace an inner function with u and its derivative with du: the chain rule run backwards.

concepts.title: Derivative of sine
concepts.summary: d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = -sin x, when x is in radians.

concepts.title: Small-angle limit
concepts.summary: sin x / x tends to 1 as x tends to 0, so sin x is about x for small x in radians.

concepts.title: Integration by parts
concepts.summary: The integral of u dv equals u v minus the integral of v du: the product rule run backwards.

concepts.title: Choosing u
concepts.summary: Choose u to be the factor that gets simpler when differentiated (a polynomial) and dv the factor you can integrate.

concepts.title: Partial sums
concepts.summary: The sum of the first n terms; the series converges when these tend to a limit.

concepts.title: Geometric series
concepts.summary: a + ar + ar^2 + ... = a / (1 - r) when |r| < 1, and diverges otherwise.

concepts.title: p-series
concepts.summary: The sum of 1/n^p converges for p > 1 and diverges for p <= 1; the harmonic series (p = 1) diverges.

concepts.title: Ratio test
concepts.summary: If |a(n+1)/a(n)| tends to L, the series converges when L < 1 and diverges when L > 1.

concepts.title: Alternating series test
concepts.summary: If terms alternate in sign, decrease in size and tend to zero, the series converges.

concepts.title: Error bound
concepts.summary: The error after n terms is at most the size of the first omitted term.

concepts.title: Power series
concepts.summary: A sum of c(n) (x - a)^n: a polynomial that never stops, whose behaviour depends on x.

concepts.title: Radius of convergence
concepts.summary: The R for which the series converges when |x - a| < R and diverges when |x - a| > R; the ratio test finds it.

concepts.title: Taylor series
concepts.summary: f(x) = sum of [f^(n)(a) / n!] times (x - a)^n; at a = 0, e^x = sum of x^n / n!.

concepts.title: Error bound
concepts.summary: If |f^(n+1)| <= M on the interval, the error of the degree-n polynomial is at most M |x|^(n+1) / (n+1)!.

concepts.title: Integrate term by term
concepts.summary: A power series can be integrated inside its radius, giving series for integrals with no elementary antiderivative.

concepts.title: Approximation by truncation
concepts.summary: Keep the leading terms where later ones are negligible: sin x ≈ x, 1/(1 + x) ≈ 1 - x.

concepts.title: Differential equation
concepts.summary: An equation relating a function to its derivatives; a solution is a function that satisfies it.

concepts.title: Exponential model
concepts.summary: dy/dt = k y has solutions y = y0 e^(kt): doubling time ln 2 / k when k > 0, half-life ln 2 / |k| when k < 0.

concepts.title: Separable equation
concepts.summary: dy/dx = f(x) g(y) can be rewritten as dy/g(y) = f(x) dx and integrated on both sides.

concepts.title: Initial condition
concepts.summary: A value y(x0) = y0 fixes the constant in the general solution.

concepts.title: Euler's method
concepts.summary: Starting at (x0, y0), take steps y(n+1) = y(n) + h f(x(n), y(n)).

concepts.title: Step size and error
concepts.summary: Smaller steps follow the true curve more closely; Euler's error shrinks roughly in proportion to h.

concepts.title: Logistic equation
concepts.summary: dP/dt = r P (1 - P / K): growth that slows as P approaches the carrying capacity K.

concepts.title: Equilibria
concepts.summary: Constant solutions where dP/dt = 0: P = 0 (unstable) and P = K (stable).

concepts.title: Second-order linear equation
concepts.summary: A constant-coefficient equation y'' + a y' + b y = 0 has solutions e^(r t) where r solves r^2 + a r + b = 0.

concepts.title: Oscillation
concepts.summary: Complex roots give oscillation; for y'' + w^2 y = 0 the solutions are cos(w t) and sin(w t) with period 2 pi / w.

lessons.title: Growth that feeds itself

reveal.text: The total creeps up to 2.717 and no further than $e = 2.71828$, however many payments there are.

lead.text: The totals in the figure come from the formula $(1+\tfrac1n)^n$, and the limit they approach is written $e$, with $e = 2.71828\ldots$. That number is where the growth in the opening stops, and it also turns up in a different place, in the slope of an exponential curve $y = a^x$ at the point $x = 0$. To find a slope at a point you take the [[derivative|The slope of a curve at a point, as a limit of slopes over shorter and shorter intervals. Met in Calculus: Change and Accumulation.]], so the slope at 0 is the limit of $\dfrac{a^h - 1}{h}$ as $h$ shrinks, because $a^0 = 1$.

Taking $h = 0.001$ gives about 0.693 for $a = 2$ and about 1.099 for $a = 3$. The slope grows with the base, so somewhere between 2 and 3 there is a base whose slope at 0 is exactly 1, and the figure shows where. That base is **$e$**, the same number that compounding produced, and it is the reason $e$ is not just another constant: it is **the base whose curve has slope 1 at $x = 0$**.

afterFigure.text: Every base has a slope at 0, and only $e$ makes it equal to the height of the curve there, which is 1.

diagram.alt: A curve of the slope of a to the power x at x equals 0, against the base a, for a from 1.5 to 4. The curve rises from 0.41 to 1.39 and crosses the height 1 at a equal to e, about 2.718.
diagram.caption: The slope at 0 grows with the base. It equals 1 at one base only, and that base is e.

reveal.text: The slope is well above 1, as it is for every base larger than $e$, so the base with slope exactly 1 lies below 3, which is where the figure puts $e$.
The slope at $x = 1$ is 2.718, the same as the height. The next screen shows why the slope tracks the height all along the curve.

lead.text: Write $a^{x+h} = a^x \cdot a^h$. The slope of $a^x$ at the point $x$ is the limit of $\dfrac{a^{x+h} - a^x}{h} = a^x \cdot \dfrac{a^h - 1}{h}$, and the second factor is exactly the slope at 0 from the previous screen. So for every base, **the slope at $x$ is the height $a^x$ multiplied by the slope at 0**.
For $a = e$ the slope at 0 is 1, which leaves $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x$. The function is its own derivative.

afterFigure.text: The rule $\dfrac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}$ is for a variable base with a fixed exponent, whereas in $e^x$ the variable sits in the exponent, so the answer is not $xe^{x-1}$. When the exponent is a multiple of $x$ the [[chain rule|The derivative of f(g(x)) is f′(g(x)) times g′(x). Met in Calculus: Change and Accumulation.]] supplies the extra factor: $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{kx} = ke^{kx}$, because the inner function $kx$ has derivative $k$.

diagram.alt: The curve y equals e to the x with a straight tangent line drawn at x equals 0, 1 or 2. At each point the printed slope of the tangent equals the printed height of the curve.
diagram.caption: The curve y = e^x and its tangent. Switch the point and compare the slope with the height.

steps.headline: Find the slope of $y = e^{2x}$ at $x = 1$.

workedSteps.text: The exponent is $2x$, so the inner function is $2x$ and its derivative is 2.
The derivative of $e^u$ is $e^u$ times $u'$, so the derivative of $e^{2x}$ is $2e^{2x}$.
Put $x = 1$ into the result, which gives $2e^2$.
The exact slope $2e^2$ can also be written as a decimal.

lead.text: A logarithm answers the question that an exponential poses the other way round: $\ln x$ is the power to which $e$ must be raised to give $x$, so $e^{\ln x} = x$ and $\ln(e^x) = x$. It is called the **natural logarithm** and it is the logarithm to base $e$, which is why it is not the same function as $\log_{10}x$, the power of 10 that gives $x$.

To differentiate it, let $y = \ln x$, so that $e^y = x$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ gives $e^y \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$ by the chain rule, hence $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{e^y} = \dfrac1x$. The result is **$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln x = \dfrac1x$**.

afterFigure.text: The same idea differentiates any exponential base. Since $a = e^{\ln a}$, we can write $a^x = e^{x\ln a}$, and the chain rule with $k = \ln a$ gives $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\ln a$.

reveal.text: The slope is $\tfrac14$, and at $x = 8$ it would be $\tfrac18$: the natural logarithm keeps rising, but ever more slowly.

workedSteps.text: Rewrite the base using $2 = e^{\ln 2}$, so that $2^x = e^{x\ln 2}$.
Differentiate with the chain rule, where $k = \ln 2$, which gives $\ln 2$ times $e^{x\ln 2}$.
The slope is the value of this derivative at $x = 2$.

lead.text: The same method differentiates a logarithm to another base, because $\log_{10}x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}$ and $\ln 10$ is a constant.

reveal.text: The factor $\tfrac1{\ln 10}$ is why base-10 logarithms rise more slowly than natural ones: at every $x$ their slope is 0.434 times as large.

lessons.orientation: Differentiate exponentials and logarithms, and see why the number e is the natural base.
lessons.nextAction: Differentiate a product and integrate by substitution, so that expressions like $x e^{x}$ and $2x e^{x^2}$ are within reach.

blocks.text: In 1683 Jacob Bernoulli asked what happens to money earning 100% interest a year when the interest is added more often than once. With a single payment at the end of the year, £1 becomes £2. Paid in two halves, so that the first half earns interest of its own, the total is $(1 + \tfrac12)^2 = 2.25$; paid monthly it is $(1+\tfrac1{12})^{12} = 2.613$, and paid daily it is $(1+\tfrac1{365})^{365} = 2.7146$.
Each splitting adds less than the one before, and the total does not grow without limit: it closes in on a fixed number, which Leonhard Euler named $e$ in a manuscript of about 1727 to 1728.

diagram.alt: Thirty points showing the value of one pound after a year of 100 percent interest, paid n times a year, for n from 1 to 30. The points rise quickly from 2 and level off toward a dashed line at 2.71828.
diagram.caption: The total after one year for n payments a year. It keeps rising but never reaches the dashed line at e.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to differentiate $e^{kx}$, $a^x$ and $\ln x$, and say why $e$ is the base calculus prefers.
intro.whyItMatters: Exponentials describe growth, cooling and decay, and every differential equation later in this course leans on their derivatives.

recap.keyIdea: The derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$ because $e$ is the base whose slope at 0 equals its height, and $\ln x$ undoes it, with derivative $1/x$.

blocks.text: Every exponential $a^x$ has a slope at 0, and $e$ is the one base for which that slope is exactly 1. Because the slope at any point is the height there times the slope at 0, $e^x$ has the derivative $e^x$, the chain rule makes it $ke^{kx}$ for $e^{kx}$, and $a^x$ gives $a^x\ln a$.
The natural logarithm $\ln x$ undoes $e^x$ and has derivative $\tfrac1x$, while other logarithms differ from it by a constant factor.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson differentiates products such as $xe^x$ and reverses the chain rule to integrate.

lessons.title: Products and substitution

reveal.text: The area grows by about 2%: each side adds a strip worth 1% of the area, and the small corner where the two strips overlap is only 0.01%. The next screen turns that picture into a rule.

lead.text: Take two quantities $u$ and $v$ that both depend on $x$, and think of their product as the area of a rectangle with sides $u$ and $v$. When $x$ changes a little, $u$ grows by $du$ and $v$ grows by $dv$. The first strip added, along the side of length $v$, has area $v\,du$, and the second, along the side of length $u$, has area $u\,dv$. The area gained is these two strips, plus a small corner of area $du\,dv$.

The corner is a product of two small quantities, so it shrinks much faster than the strips and vanishes in the limit. Dividing the two strips by the change in $x$ gives the **product rule**: $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, **one factor differentiated at a time, the other left alone**.

afterFigure.text: Check the rule on $x^2 = x\cdot x$, where $u = v = x$ and $u' = v' = 1$. It gives $1\cdot x + x\cdot 1 = 2x$, which agrees with the power rule and corrects the tempting rule, which would have given 1. For $xe^x$ it gives $1\cdot e^x + x\cdot e^x = (1+x)e^x$.

diagram.alt: A rectangle with sides u and v. A strip of width du along the right side adds du times v; a strip of height dv along the top adds u times dv; when both grow there is also a small corner du times dv.
diagram.caption: The area uv changes by strips. Switch between the sides that grow.

steps.headline: Find the slope of $y = xe^x$ at $x = 1$.

workedSteps.text: Name the two factors and differentiate each one.
workedSteps.math: u = x,\ u' = 1;\quad v = e^x,\ v' = e^x

workedSteps.text: Apply $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, using the fact that $e^x$ is its own derivative.
Put $x = 1$ into the result.
The exact slope $2e$ can also be written as a decimal.

reveal.text: The derivative is $(2x + x^2)e^x$, so the slope at $x = 1$ is $3e$, which is 8.15.

lead.text: The chain rule says that $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{x^2} = 2x\,e^{x^2}$, so the antiderivative of $2x\,e^{x^2}$ must be $e^{x^2}$. Substitution is the method that finds such an antiderivative without having to guess it. Name the inner function, $u = x^2$, and notice that its differential is $du = 2x\,dx$, which is exactly the piece of the integrand that sits beside the exponential. The integral $\int 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx$ then becomes $\int e^u\,du$.

That is the rule in general: **substitution works when the derivative of the inner part is also present** in the integrand, apart from a constant factor. If $\int 3x\,e^{x^2}dx$ were asked instead, the factor would be adjusted, since $x\,dx = \tfrac12du$ turns it into $\tfrac32\int e^u\,du$.

afterFigure.text: From $x = 0$ to $x = 1$ the variable $u = x^2$ also runs from 0 to 1, and the area under $2x\,e^{x^2}$ in $x$ equals the area under $e^u$ in $u$, which is $e - 1 = 1.718$. The two graphs look different, but they enclose the same area, so changing variables changes the picture and not the answer.

diagram.alt: Two views with the same shaded area of 1.718. One plots 2x times e to the x squared for x from 0 to 1; the other plots e to the u for u from 0 to 1.
diagram.caption: The same area, 1.718, in two coordinates. Substituting u = x² turns the first graph into the second.

reveal.text: The limits are $x = 0 \mapsto u = 1$ and $x = 2 \mapsto u = 5$: they belong to the variable that is being integrated.

workedSteps.text: Let $u = x^2+1$, so $du = 2x\,dx$ and $x\,dx = \tfrac12du$.
Change the limits with the same formula: $x = 0$ gives $u = 1$, and $x = 2$ gives $u = 5$.
The integral is now $\tfrac12\int_1^5\dfrac{du}{u}$, and an antiderivative of $1/u$ is $\ln u$.

lead.text: Compare $\int x\,e^{x^2}\,dx$ with $\int e^{x^2}\,dx$. In the first, $u = x^2$ leaves $x\,dx = \tfrac12du$ exactly as needed, and the answer is $\tfrac12e^{x^2}$. In the second there is no $x$ beside the exponential, so naming $u = x^2$ would leave $dx = du/(2\sqrt u)$, which makes the integral harder and not easier. The inner function must come with its derivative, and no choice of letter can supply a factor that is missing.

In practice, look for a composite expression, such as $e^{x^2}$, $(1+x^2)^3$ or $\dfrac1{x^2+1}$, and check whether the derivative of its inside appears elsewhere in the integrand. When it does, set $u$ to the inside, and when it does not, another method is needed.

reveal.text: In $\int \dfrac{x}{x^2+4}\,dx$ the factor $x\,dx$ is half of $du$ for $u = x^2 + 4$; the other two integrals have no such partner.

lead.text: In the earlier example the factor 2 stood beside the exponential, and here it is missing.

reveal.text: The missing 2 makes the answer half as large, $\tfrac12(e-1)$, because $x\,dx$ is $\tfrac12du$.

lessons.orientation: Differentiate a product with the product rule and integrate with a substitution.
lessons.nextAction: Differentiate sine and cosine and see why a small angle in radians is nearly equal to its sine.

blocks.text: The derivative of $x^2$ is $2x$, yet $x^2$ is the product $x\cdot x$, and each of its factors has derivative 1. A tempting rule says that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives, which would give $x^2$ a slope of 1 at every point, so the derivative of a product must carry more information than the two derivatives alone, and the extra information is what the **product rule** supplies.

Reading the chain rule backwards gives a matching idea for integrals. Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{x^2} = 2x\,e^{x^2}$, the integral of $2x\,e^{x^2}$ is $e^{x^2}$, and any integrand that holds an inner function with its own derivative beside it can be integrated in the same way, by a method called **substitution**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to differentiate a product and to integrate by substitution, including changing the limits of a definite integral.
intro.whyItMatters: Products and composite functions occur whenever two changing quantities interact, so these two rules open most of the functions in later lessons.

recap.keyIdea: The product rule is $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, and substitution reverses the chain rule when an inner function appears with its derivative.

blocks.text: A product of two changing quantities changes through two strips of area, one per factor, so its derivative is $u'v + uv'$. Substitution takes an integrand of the form $f(u)\,u'$ and integrates $f$ over $u$, with the limits of a definite integral changed along with the variable.
The method fails when the derivative of the inner function is absent, which is the case that the next lessons handle by other means.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson differentiates sine and cosine, which depend on the same limit idea and give oscillation its calculus.

lessons.title: Calculus of sine and cosine

reveal.text: The value is 0.1987, only slightly less than the angle 0.2 itself, and the next screen explains why the two stay so close.

lead.text: On the unit circle an angle of $x$ radians cuts off an arc of length $x$, and the sine is the height of the point at the end of the arc. For a small angle the arc is almost a straight vertical line, so its length $x$ and the height $\sin x$ nearly agree. Numbers show the same thing: $\sin 0.5 \div 0.5 = 0.9589$, $\sin 0.1 \div 0.1 = 0.99833$, and $\sin 0.01 \div 0.01 = 0.999983$.

The ratio closes in on 1, which is written $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$. This limit says that **the slope of the sine curve at 0 is exactly 1**, because that slope is the limit of $\dfrac{\sin h - \sin 0}{h}$. The statement holds only for radians, since an arc of length $x$ requires $x$ to be a length on the unit circle.

afterFigure.text: The approximation $\sin x \approx x$ is good enough for many uses. It is within 1% of the true ratio while $x$ is below about 0.245 radians, or 14 degrees, which is why a pendulum swinging through a few degrees behaves in a simple way.

diagram.alt: Two views of the sine function near zero. In the first, the curves y equals x and y equals sin x lie on top of each other close to 0. In the second, the graph of sin x divided by x approaches 1 as x approaches 0.
diagram.caption: Left to right, sin x falls behind x, but near 0 the ratio sin x ÷ x is almost exactly 1.

reveal.text: The error is about 0.0045, only 1.5% of the angle, and it grows quickly for larger angles, since it behaves like $x^3/6$.
The inner function $2x$ has derivative 2, so the derivative is $2\cos 2x$: the wave oscillates twice as fast and its slope is twice as steep.

lead.text: The slope of sine at a general point comes from the angle-addition formula, $\sin(x+h) = \sin x\cos h + \cos x\sin h$, which was met in [[Trigonometry|The sine of a sum of two angles is sin x cos h + cos x sin h.]]. The slope is $\dfrac{\sin(x+h) - \sin x}{h} = \sin x\cdot\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x\cdot\dfrac{\sin h}{h}$. As $h$ tends to 0 the second fraction tends to 1 by the limit above, and the first tends to 0, since $\cos h - 1$ is far smaller than $h$. What remains is $\cos x$.
So **$\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$**, and the same method gives $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$.

afterFigure.text: Both formulas rely on radians, and in degrees an extra factor appears. A degree is $\pi/180$ of a radian, so the slope of $\sin x$ at $x = 0$ with $x$ in degrees is $\pi/180 = 0.01745$, not 1. The chain rule also matters for a multiple of the angle: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin 3x = 3\cos 3x$.

diagram.alt: The sine curve in blue with its tangent line in orange at one chosen point, and the cosine curve dashed in green. At each chosen point the slope of the tangent equals the value of cosine there, which is marked by a green dot.
diagram.caption: The slope of sin x at each point equals the height of cos x there. Switch the point.

workedSteps.text: The inner function is $3x$, whose derivative is 3.
The derivative of $\sin u$ is $\cos u$ times $u'$.
At $x = \pi/9$ the angle $3x$ equals $\pi/3$, and $\cos(\pi/3) = \tfrac12$.
The derivative $3\cos 3x$ takes one value at this point.

lead.text: Reading the derivatives backwards gives $\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x$ and $\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x$. The chain rule in reverse is substitution, so for $\cos kx$ the inner function $u = kx$ leaves $dx = du/k$, and $\int \cos kx\,dx = \dfrac{\sin kx}{k}$.

For the area under one half-wave, $\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx = \bigl[-\cos x\bigr]_0^{\pi} = 1 - (-1) = 2$. The symmetry of the sine curve makes the area over a *full* period cancel, because the second half-wave lies below the axis and counts as negative, but over $0$ to $\pi$ nothing cancels.

afterFigure.text: The first half-wave has area exactly 2, and the full period from 0 to $2\pi$ gives $2 + (-2) = 0$, which is a *signed* area, so zero here does not mean that the region is empty.

diagram.alt: The sine curve from 0 to 2π. In the first view the region under the first half-wave, from 0 to π, is shaded and has area 2. In the second view the region between the second half-wave and the axis is also shaded, and counts as negative 2, so the total over a full period is 0.
diagram.caption: The first half-wave has area 2. Over a full period the two half-waves cancel.

reveal.text: The antiderivative is $\tfrac12\sin 2x$, and at $x = \pi/4$ the angle is $\pi/2$, where the sine is 1.

workedSteps.text: An antiderivative of $\sin kx$ is $-\dfrac{\cos kx}{k}$, so here it is $-\tfrac12\cos 2x$.
The integral is the antiderivative at the upper limit minus the antiderivative at the lower limit.

reveal.text: The acceleration is $-9$ times the position, since $x'' = -18\sin 3t$ and $x = 2\sin 3t$. This pattern, acceleration proportional to minus the position, returns in the last lesson.

lessons.orientation: Differentiate and integrate sine and cosine, and use the small-angle limit.
lessons.nextAction: Integrate a product such as $x e^x$ or $x\sin x$, which substitution cannot reach, by reversing the product rule.

blocks.text: The sine of 0.1 radians is 0.0998334, so close to 0.1 that a calculator display barely shows the gap, and the sine of 0.01 is 0.00999983, closer still. Because the radian is a length on the unit circle, the arc of a small angle and the height of its point are almost the same thing, and the approximation $\sin x \approx x$ gets better as the angle shrinks.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to differentiate and integrate sine and cosine in radians, and use $\sin x \approx x$ for small angles.
intro.whyItMatters: Waves, orbits and vibrations are built from sine and cosine, and this pair of derivatives is the reason an oscillator's acceleration points back to its centre.

recap.keyIdea: In radians, $\sin x$ has derivative $\cos x$ and $\cos x$ has derivative $-\sin x$, because $\sin x / x \to 1$ as $x \to 0$.

blocks.text: The limit $\sin x / x \to 1$ gives the slope of sine at 0, and the angle-addition formula carries it to every other point, so the derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$ and that of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. The chain rule scales the result by the factor of the angle, and reading the formulas backwards gives $\int\cos kx\,dx = \sin kx/k$.
These formulas hold for radians only, since in degrees an extra factor $\pi/180$ appears, and an integral over a half-wave is positive even though a full period gives a signed total of zero.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reverses the product rule to integrate products such as $x\cos x$, which substitution cannot reach.

lessons.title: Integrating a product

reveal.text: The shortcut gives 0.859, but the area is exactly 1, so the integral of a product is *not* the product of the integrals.

lead.text: The product rule says $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$. Integrating both sides turns the left into $uv$ and splits the right into two integrals, so $uv = \int v\,u'\,dx + \int u\,v'\,dx$. Writing $du = u'\,dx$ and $dv = v'\,dx$ and moving one integral to the other side gives the formula **$\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$**, which is called **integration by parts**.

What the formula buys is a change of problem. The original integral has $u$ times the differential of $v$, and the new one has $v$ times the differential of $u$. If differentiating $u$ makes it simpler and integrating $dv$ gives no trouble, the new integral is easier than the old one.

afterFigure.text: The formula applies to a definite integral too, with the term $uv$ evaluated at both limits, and that boundary term must not be dropped.

reveal.text: Choosing $u = x$ leaves $\int e^x\,dx$, and the next screen shows what the other choices leave.

workedSteps.text: The integrand is a product of two factors. The formula $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$ needs one of them as $u$ and the other, with $dx$, as $dv$.
Take $u = x$, which becomes simpler when differentiated, and $dv = e^x\,dx$, which is easy to integrate. Then $du = dx$ and $v = e^x$.
workedSteps.math: u = x,\ du = dx;\quad dv = e^x\,dx,\ v = e^x

workedSteps.text: Apply the formula, keeping the boundary term $uv$.
Evaluate the boundary term, $2e^2 - 0$, and the remaining integral, $e^2 - 1$.
The two parts combine into one value, which can be written as a decimal.

lead.text: For $\int x\,e^x\,dx$ both splits are legal, since the formula never refuses. With $u = x$ we get $du = dx$ and $v = e^x$, and the leftover integral $\int e^x\,dx$ is one step from the answer. With $u = e^x$ we get $du = e^x\,dx$, and $dv = x\,dx$ gives $v = \tfrac{x^2}{2}$, so the leftover integral is $\int \tfrac{x^2}{2}e^x\,dx$, which has a *higher* power of $x$ than the integral we began with.

A polynomial is the usual choice for $u$, because differentiating it lowers its degree and eventually reaches a constant. Exponentials and sine or cosine are the usual choices for $dv$, since they integrate to something of the same kind. **The wrong choice does not make the method fail, only make the new integral harder**, which is the signal to go back and swap the roles.

afterFigure.text: The result for $\int x\,e^x\,dx$ is $xe^x - e^x = (x-1)e^x$, and differentiating it with the product rule gives back $xe^x$, which is a check that always works for an antiderivative.

diagram.alt: Two ways of splitting the integral of x times e to the x into u and dv. With u equal to x the leftover integral is just the integral of e to the x. With u equal to e to the x the leftover integral contains x squared and is harder.
diagram.caption: Both splits are legal, but only one leaves a simpler integral. Switch between them.

reveal.text: The antiderivative is $\tfrac12xe^{2x} - \tfrac14e^{2x}$, and the limits 0 and 1 give $\tfrac14(e^2 + 1)$.

lead.text: Take $\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx$ with $u = x$ and $dv = \sin x\,dx$, so that $du = dx$ and $v = -\cos x$. The formula gives $\bigl[-x\cos x\bigr]_0^\pi + \int_0^\pi \cos x\,dx$. The boundary term is $-\pi\cos\pi - 0 = \pi$, and the remaining integral is $\sin\pi - \sin 0 = 0$, so the total is $\pi$, or 3.142.

Here the new integral contributes nothing at all, so **the whole answer comes from the boundary term**. A learner who dropped it, thinking that only the integral on the right does the work, would have found 0, and the figure shows that the area is plainly not zero.

afterFigure.text: The same care applies to signs. Because $v = -\cos x$ carries a minus sign, the second integral is added and not subtracted: the formula subtracts $\int v\,du = -\int\cos x\,dx$.

diagram.alt: The curve y equals x sin x for x from 0 to pi, with the area beneath it shaded. The area is pi, about 3.142.
diagram.caption: The area under x sin x from 0 to π is exactly π.

workedSteps.text: Take $u = x$ and $dv = \cos x\,dx$, so that $du = dx$ and $v = \sin x$.
workedSteps.math: u = x,\ du = dx;\quad v = \sin x

workedSteps.text: The formula gives a boundary term and a remaining integral, and both are evaluated between the limits.

lead.text: Consider $\int_0^1 x^2e^x\,dx$. With $u = x^2$ and $dv = e^x\,dx$ the formula gives $\bigl[x^2e^x\bigr]_0^1 - \int_0^1 2x\,e^x\,dx = e - 2\int_0^1 xe^x\,dx$. The remaining integral is the one from the opening, which equals 1, so the answer is $e - 2 = 0.718$.
Each pass lowers the power of $x$ by one, and the integral ends when the power reaches zero. For $x^3e^x$ three passes are needed, and for $x^n e^x$ the pattern continues with $n$ passes.

reveal.text: Here $v = -e^{-x}$, so the integral is $\bigl[-xe^{-x}\bigr]_0^1 + \int_0^1 e^{-x}\,dx = 1 - 2/e$, which is 0.264.

lessons.orientation: Use integration by parts on products of a polynomial with an exponential or a sine.
lessons.nextAction: Add up a sequence of terms that never ends, starting with the partial sums of a geometric series.

blocks.text: The area under $y = xe^x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 1$ is a plain question, yet substitution cannot answer it: the derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$ and not $x$, so no inner function has its derivative standing beside it. The area is nevertheless a definite number, and it turns out to be exactly 1.

The method that reaches it is the product rule turned around. The rule writes the derivative of a product as two terms, and rearranging it so that an integral appears on each side gives a way to trade a hard integral for an easier one, which is called **integration by parts**.

diagram.alt: The curve y equals x times e to the x for x from 0 to 1, with the area beneath it shaded. The area is exactly 1.
diagram.caption: The area under x e^x from 0 to 1 is exactly 1, even though no single substitution produces it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to integrate a polynomial times an exponential or a sine by parts, choosing $u$ well and keeping the boundary term.
intro.whyItMatters: Parts is the second standard method after substitution, and it turns up again whenever a polynomial multiplies a wave or an exponential.

recap.keyIdea: Integration by parts is $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$, and it works best when $u$ is the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated.

blocks.text: Parts is the product rule integrated, and it exchanges $\int u\,dv$ for $uv - \int v\,du$. A polynomial is the usual choice for $u$ because each differentiation lowers its degree, and a polynomial of higher degree needs repeated passes.
In a definite integral the boundary term $uv$ is evaluated at both limits and must be kept, because it can carry part or all of the answer.

lessons.title: Adding forever

reveal.text: Five pieces cover $\tfrac{31}{32} = 0.969$ of the square: only a sliver of area $\tfrac1{32}$ is left over.

lead.text: The sum $\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \cdots$ is an example of a **series**, which is a sum whose terms continue without end. You cannot add infinitely many numbers one at a time, so the sum is *defined* through the totals that can be worked out: the **partial sums**, $S_1 = \tfrac12$, $S_2 = \tfrac34$, $S_3 = \tfrac78$, and in general $S_n$ is the sum of the first $n$ terms.

In the square, $S_n$ is the area covered after $n$ pieces, and it equals $1 - \tfrac1{2^n}$, which is the whole square less the last gap. The gap halves at every step and tends to 0, so the partial sums tend to 1. When the partial sums tend to a limit, the series **converges** to that limit, and the limit is called its sum.

afterFigure.text: A common belief is that adding infinitely many positive numbers must give infinity. The square shows otherwise, because the terms shrink fast enough for the total to stay below 1.

reveal.text: The partial sum is $2 - \tfrac1{32}$, which is just under 2, and the next screen shows where the partial sums are heading.

lead.text: In a **geometric series** each term is the one before multiplied by a fixed ratio $r$. To find $S_n = a + ar + \cdots + ar^{n-1}$, multiply it by $r$ to get $rS_n = ar + ar^2 + \cdots + ar^n$. Almost every term appears in both, so subtracting leaves $S_n - rS_n = a - ar^n$, and therefore $S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$.

When $|r| < 1$, the power $r^n$ shrinks toward 0 as $n$ grows, and the formula settles on $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$. **The sum of a convergent geometric series is its first term over one minus its ratio.** For $a = 1$ and $r = \tfrac12$ this gives 2, which is the limit the figure shows for the climbing points, and for $r = -\tfrac12$ it gives $\tfrac23$, which the alternating points close in on from both sides.

afterFigure.text: The ratio may be negative, and then the partial sums alternate above and below the limit. The condition that matters is the size of $r$, not its sign.

steps.headline: Find the sum of $6 + 3.6 + 2.16 + \cdots$, in which each term is 0.6 of the one before.

workedSteps.text: Read off the first term and the ratio.
The ratio has size less than 1, so the series converges, and the formula applies.
That leaves a single division to carry out.

reveal.text: Only $r = -0.5$ has size less than 1; the next screen shows what the partial sums do for the others.

lead.text: For $r = 1$ every term is 1 and $S_n = n$, which grows without limit. For $r = -1$ the sums alternate between 1 and 0 and approach nothing. For $r = \tfrac32$ the term $r^n$ grows, so $S_n$ grows faster and faster. In each case the series **diverges**.

A repeating decimal shows the other side of the rule. The number $0.999\ldots$ is the series $0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + \cdots$ with $a = 0.9$ and $r = 0.1$, so its sum is $\dfrac{0.9}{1 - 0.1} = 1$, and it is not a little below 1. The same method gives any repeating decimal as a fraction.

afterFigure.text: There is a caution here. For a geometric series the terms tend to 0 exactly when $|r| < 1$, but in general terms tending to 0 is only *necessary* for convergence. The sum $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14 + \cdots$ has terms that tend to 0, and yet its partial sums grow without limit.

diagram.alt: Partial sums of a geometric series for ratios 1, minus 1 and 3 over 2. With ratio 1 the sums rise in equal steps, with ratio minus 1 they alternate between 1 and 0, and with ratio 3 over 2 they grow faster and faster. None settles on a limit.
diagram.caption: When the ratio has size 1 or more, the partial sums do not settle.

The rebound heights form a geometric series with first term 6 and ratio 0.6, which is the series summed earlier in this lesson.
Every part of that expression is now known.

lessons.orientation: Sum a geometric series and say when an infinite sum has a finite value.
lessons.nextAction: Test series that are not geometric, using the p-series and the ratio test.

blocks.text: Here is a sum that never ends: $\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \cdots$, in which every term is half the one before. Zeno of Elea used arguments of this kind in the fifth century BC to claim that motion could never be completed, saying that a walk across a room must first cover half the distance, then half of what remains, and so on, so that it seems to need infinitely many stages.

The stages never stop coming, but each one covers only half of what is left, so no number of them can take the walk past the whole distance, and an endless sum can therefore have a finite total. A sum in which each term is a fixed multiple of the one before is called a **geometric series**, and it is the model for deciding whether any other endless sum has a total at all.

diagram.caption: Each piece is half the area that remains, so the pieces never overflow the square.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sum a geometric series, say when it converges, and use partial sums to count a distance with infinitely many parts.
intro.whyItMatters: Infinite sums are how calculus defines a function through its series, and geometric series are the one case in which the total can be written down exactly.

recap.keyIdea: A series converges when its partial sums settle on a limit, and a geometric series with ratio $r$ of size less than 1 has the sum $a/(1 - r)$.

blocks.text: The partial sums of a series are the totals of its first $n$ terms, and the series converges when they approach a limit. For a geometric series $S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)$, which gives the sum $a/(1-r)$ when $|r| < 1$ and no limit otherwise.

That is enough to find the total distance of a bouncing ball and to turn a repeating decimal into a fraction. Terms that shrink to zero do not by themselves guarantee a convergent series, and the next lesson looks for tests that do.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks of series that are not geometric whether they settle, and compares the harmonic series with the p-series.

lessons.title: Does it settle?

reveal.text: The partial sums never settle: they pass 3 after eleven terms and 10 after 12,367, and the next screen explains why they cannot stop.
The sum of the first 1000 terms is 1.644: this series settles. The only difference from the harmonic series is the square in the denominator.

lead.text: Group the terms: $\tfrac13 + \tfrac14$ is more than $\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$, then $\tfrac15 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac17 + \tfrac18$ is more than $4 \times \tfrac18 = \tfrac12$, then eight terms from $\tfrac19$ to $\tfrac1{16}$ exceed $8 \times \tfrac1{16} = \tfrac12$ again.

Every block adds more than $\tfrac12$ and there are infinitely many blocks, so the sum **exceeds any number we name**. The growth is slow, since the sums behave like $\ln n$: a total above 10 needs 12,367 terms. A series whose partial sums were only inspected on a calculator could therefore look convergent for thousands of terms while it diverges.

afterFigure.text: For a series to converge its terms must tend to 0, which is a *necessary* condition. It is not a sufficient one, and the harmonic series is the standard example.

diagram.alt: Two curves of partial sums up to 1000 terms. The sum of 1 over n keeps rising, reaching 7.485, while the sum of 1 over n squared flattens near 1.64 almost at once.
diagram.caption: Both series have terms that tend to 0, but only one has partial sums that settle.

lead.text: A series of the form $\sum 1/n^p$ is called a **p-series**. The harmonic series is the case $p = 1$ and it diverges, and so does any $p$ below 1, such as $\sum 1/\sqrt n$, whose terms are larger than $1/n$. For $p = 2$ the sum converges, which we can see by comparing it with a series that telescopes. Since $\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)} = \dfrac1n - \dfrac1{n+1}$, the partial sum $\tfrac1{1\cdot2} + \tfrac1{2\cdot3} + \cdots + \tfrac1{n(n+1)}$ equals $1 - \dfrac1{n+1}$, because each negative term cancels the next positive one, and the total tends to 1.

Now $\dfrac1{n^2} \le \dfrac{2}{n(n+1)}$ for every $n \ge 1$, since this says $n + 1 \le 2n$. So the partial sums of $\sum 1/n^2$ never exceed twice the telescoping total, which is 2, and a series of positive terms whose sums are bounded must converge. **The comparison shows that $\sum 1/n^2$ converges**, and Euler showed in 1735 that its sum is exactly $\pi^2/6 = 1.645$.

afterFigure.text: The method has a name: **comparison**. A series of positive terms that is smaller than a convergent one converges, and one that is larger than a divergent one diverges. For p-series the dividing line is sharp: $p = 1$ diverges and any $p > 1$ converges.

diagram.alt: A bar of length 1 cut into successive pieces of length 1/2, 1/6, 1/12, 1/20 and so on. Together they leave only a shrinking gap at the right end, so the pieces add up to 1.
diagram.caption: Each piece is 1/n − 1/(n+1), so the pieces cancel in pairs and leave 1 − 1/(n+1).

reveal.text: Only the first and last parts survive, leaving $1 - \tfrac1{10}$, which is 0.9 and tends to 1 as more terms are added.

lead.text: A geometric series converges because each term is a fixed fraction of the last. The **ratio test** applies that idea to any series with positive terms $a_n$ by taking the limit $L$ of $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}$. If $L < 1$ the terms eventually shrink like a geometric series with ratio near $L$, so the series converges, and if $L > 1$ the terms grow and it diverges. For $\sum \dfrac{3^n}{n!}$ the ratio is $\dfrac{3^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{3^n/n!} = \dfrac{3}{n+1}$, which tends to 0, so the series converges.

The test is made for terms with factorials, or powers of a constant, where the ratio simplifies. **When $L = 1$ the test says nothing at all.** Both $\sum 1/n$ and $\sum 1/n^2$ have ratios that tend to 1, since $\dfrac{n}{n+1}$ and $\dfrac{n^2}{(n+1)^2}$ both approach 1, and yet the first diverges while the second converges.

workedSteps.text: Write the ratio of consecutive terms and simplify it.
Take the limit as $n$ grows.
$L$ is the number this ratio tends to, and it is then compared with 1.

reveal.text: The ratio is 0.4 at $n = 9$ and keeps falling toward 0, so the terms eventually shrink faster than those of any geometric series and the series converges.
The test is silent at $L = 1$: the harmonic series diverges but $\sum 1/n^2$, with the same limit, converges, so another test must decide.

lead.text: First ask whether the terms tend to 0. If they do not, the series diverges at once, and no further test is needed. If they do, that proves nothing, so the next question is whether the series is geometric or a p-series, because then the answer is read from $r$ or $p$. If it only resembles one, compare it, or telescope it when the terms split into a difference.
The ratio test comes last because it is silent in the cases that matter most, the ones whose ratios tend to 1, but it is the quickest method for terms such as $n/2^n$ or $3^n/n!$.

diagram.alt: Four numbered questions to ask in order about a series: whether the terms tend to zero, whether it is geometric or a p-series, whether it resembles a known series, and whether factorials or powers suggest the ratio test.
diagram.caption: A sensible order for choosing a test. The ratio test is last because it says nothing when its limit is 1.

lessons.nextAction: Add terms that alternate in sign, and put a bound on the error when the sum is stopped early.

blocks.text: The harmonic series $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14 + \cdots$ has terms that shrink toward 0, and its partial sums seem to slow down as they go: 2.929 after ten terms, 5.187 after a hundred, 7.485 after a thousand, and only 14.39 after a million. It would be natural to suspect that the total settles somewhere near 15.
A table of partial sums cannot settle the question, however far it goes, because a series can look settled long before it is. What decides it is an argument about the terms themselves.

diagram.alt: Two curves of partial sums up to 1000 terms. The sum of 1 over n keeps rising, reaching 7.485, while the sum of 1 over n squared flattens near 1.64 almost at once.
diagram.caption: Both series have terms that tend to 0, but only one has partial sums that settle.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose among the divergence, p-series, comparison and ratio tests, and say what each one proves.
intro.whyItMatters: Most series cannot be summed exactly, so the first question is always whether they converge at all, and a few tests answer it.

recap.keyIdea: A series converges only if its terms tend to 0, and the p-series, comparison and ratio tests decide the cases that remain.

blocks.text: Terms that tend to 0 are necessary for convergence but not sufficient, as the harmonic series shows. The series $\sum 1/n^p$ converges exactly when $p > 1$, a comparison with a convergent series shows convergence, and the ratio test reads the limit $L$ of $a_{n+1}/a_n$.

A limit below 1 means convergence, above 1 divergence, and exactly 1 means that the ratio test is silent. The series that are best handled by the ratio test are those with factorials and with powers of a constant.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at series whose terms alternate in sign, and at how far off a partial sum can be.

lessons.title: Alternating sums and how wrong you are

reveal.text: The sum of four terms is 0.5833. Adding the fifth term would move the total up again, and the next screen explains what these two sums have to do with the answer.

lead.text: The series $1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 + \cdots$ is the harmonic series with every other sign reversed, and the change is enough to make it converge: the partial sums in the figure at the start of the lesson zigzag, each one overshooting the limit by less than the last, and they close in on $\ln 2 = 0.6931$. A series whose signs alternate is called an **alternating series**, and the **alternating series test** says that it converges if its terms **alternate, decrease in size, and tend to zero**.

The three conditions can fail separately. $\sum(-1)^n$ alternates but its terms do not tend to 0, so its sums keep bouncing between 0 and $-1$. $\sum\dfrac1n$ decreases to 0 but does not alternate, and diverges. Decreasing terms alone are not enough, since all three conditions are needed together.

The overshooting gives more than convergence. Because each step goes past the limit by less than the previous step, **consecutive partial sums always trap the limit between them**, as the second view of that opening figure shows after four terms.

reveal.text: Only $\sum(-1)^n/n$ meets all three: its terms change sign, they decrease, and $\tfrac1n$ tends to 0.
The limit lies between 0.5833 and 0.7833, so even without knowing it, the two sums locate it to within 0.2.

lead.text: If the limit lies between any two consecutive partial sums, then the distance from $S_n$ to the limit is smaller than the distance from $S_n$ to $S_{n+1}$. That distance is the single term $a_{n+1}$ that was added to go from one to the other. So **the error after $n$ terms is no larger than the next term**, $|S - S_n| \le a_{n+1}$.

For the series above, stopping after four terms gives $S_4 = 0.5833$ and the first omitted term is $\tfrac15 = 0.2$, so the sum lies between $0.5833$ and $0.7833$. The actual error is $0.6931 - 0.5833 = 0.110$, safely inside the bound.

afterFigure.text: Most convergent series cannot be added exactly, so the real question is how many terms to take, and here the answer can be read off the terms without knowing the sum.

diagram.alt: A number line from 0.45 to 0.85 with two consecutive partial sums of the alternating harmonic series, one on each side of the limit ln 2. The shaded band between them has width equal to the first term that was left out.
diagram.caption: Consecutive partial sums trap the limit between them. The band is as wide as the first omitted term.

steps.headline: How many terms of $1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \cdots$ guarantee an error below 0.05?

workedSteps.text: After $N$ terms the error is at most the next term, which is $\dfrac1{N+1}$.
Require that bound to be strictly below 0.05, which sets a lower limit on $N + 1$.
Solving for $N$ must give a whole number of terms.

reveal.text: The first omitted term is $\tfrac1{25}$, so the error is at most 0.04. Because the terms shrink as $1/n^2$, this series closes in much faster than the alternating harmonic one.

lead.text: If the terms of $1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \cdots$ are taken without their signs, the result is the harmonic series, which diverges. A series that converges but whose positive-term version diverges is called **conditionally convergent**, while one that still converges with every sign made positive, such as $1 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac19 - \cdots$, is **absolutely convergent**.

The difference matters because of order. Rearranging the terms of an absolutely convergent series never changes its sum, but rearranging a conditionally convergent one can. Reordering the alternating harmonic series so that two positive terms are followed by one negative term, $1 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac15 + \tfrac17 - \tfrac14 + \cdots$, gives the sum $\tfrac32\ln 2 = 1.040$ and not $\ln 2$.

steps.headline: How many terms of $1 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac19 - \cdots$ guarantee an error below 0.001?

workedSteps.text: After $N$ terms the error is at most the next term, $\dfrac{1}{(N+1)^2}$.
Require this to be below 0.001, which means $(N+1)^2 > 1000$, so $N + 1$ must exceed $\sqrt{1000}$.
The root is not a whole number, and $N$ counts whole terms.

reveal.text: The first omitted term is $\tfrac1{120}$, so the error is at most 0.0083. The sum is $e^{-1} = 0.3679$, and the partial sum 0.375 is already within 0.0071 of it.

blocks.text: Add $1 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 + \cdots$ one term at a time and the running total swings above and below its final value, each swing smaller than the one before. The harmonic series, with the same terms and no minus signs, diverges, so the signs are doing something that cannot be seen from the sizes of the terms.
The totals close in on $\ln 2 = 0.6931$ from both sides without ever reaching it exactly, so any partial sum is slightly wrong.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply the alternating series test, bound the error after $n$ terms, and say how many terms a target needs.
intro.whyItMatters: Most infinite sums cannot be found exactly, and an error bound is what turns a partial sum into a result that can be trusted.

recap.keyIdea: An alternating series with shrinking terms that tend to zero converges, and stopping after $n$ terms leaves an error no larger than the next term.

blocks.text: When the signs alternate and the terms decrease and tend to 0, consecutive partial sums fall on opposite sides of the limit. The limit is therefore trapped between them, and the error after $n$ terms is at most the first omitted term, which gives the number of terms needed for any target.
Convergence that depends on the alternating signs is conditional, and for such a series the order of the terms can change the sum.

lessons.title: Power series

reveal.text: The sum is 1.25, which is the value of $\dfrac{1}{1 - 0.2}$. The next screen asks what happens when $x$ is allowed to vary.

lead.text: A sum of the form $c_0 + c_1(x - a) + c_2(x - a)^2 + \cdots$ is called a **power series** with centre $a$, and it defines a value for every $x$ at which it converges. The simplest example has every $c_n$ equal to 1 and centre 0, which is the geometric series $1 + x + x^2 + \cdots$ with ratio $x$. By the formula $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ its sum is $\dfrac{1}{1-x}$, **but only where $|x| < 1$**.

Stopping at degree 2, 4 or 8 gives a polynomial, and inside $-1 < x < 1$ each one follows $\dfrac{1}{1-x}$ more closely as the degree rises. Outside, the polynomials climb away from the function instead of approaching it, because the series diverges for $|x| \ge 1$.

afterFigure.text: So a power series is not the same thing as its function everywhere: it equals the function **inside its region of convergence**, and the question of how large that region is has a definite answer, found with the ratio test.

diagram.alt: Graphs of the partial sums 1 plus x plus x squared and so on, of degree 2, 4 or 8, drawn against the function 1 over 1 minus x. Between minus 1 and 1 the polynomial follows the function more closely as the degree rises; beyond x equal to 1 the polynomials climb away and the function does not.
diagram.caption: The polynomial hugs 1/(1 − x) inside |x| < 1 and leaves it outside. Switch the degree.

reveal.text: The function has a perfectly good value there, but the series adds 1, 3, 9, 27 and so on, which grows without limit and so has no sum. The series and the function agree only where the series converges.

lead.text: For the series $\sum \dfrac{x^n}{4^n}$ the ratio of consecutive terms is $\left|\dfrac{x^{n+1}/4^{n+1}}{x^n/4^n}\right| = \dfrac{|x|}{4}$, which does not depend on $n$. The [[ratio test|If the limit L of |a(n+1)/a(n)| is below 1 the series converges, above 1 it diverges, and at exactly 1 the test says nothing. Met in 'Does it settle?'.]] says that the series converges when this is below 1 and diverges when it is above 1, so it converges when $|x| < 4$. The number 4 is the **radius of convergence**, $R = 4$.

The test does this for any power series: take the limit of $|c_{n+1}x^{n+1}/c_nx^n|$, which has the form $|x|/R$, and **solve $|x|/R < 1$**. When the series is centred at $a$ the condition is $|x - a| < R$, so the set of $x$ that works is an interval of half-width $R$ around $a$, called the **interval of convergence**.
For the geometric series every coefficient is 1 and the ratio is $|x|$, so $R = 1$. At the two points $x = a \pm R$ the ratio test gives 1 and says nothing.

steps.headline: Find the interval of convergence of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(x-1)^n}{2^n}$.

workedSteps.text: The ratio of consecutive terms is a constant times $|x - 1|$.
The series converges when that is below 1, which gives $|x - 1| < 2$.
The interval is symmetric about its centre.

lead.text: Three series with the same radius, $R = 1$, show the point. $\sum x^n$ diverges at both $x = 1$ and $x = -1$, because its terms do not tend to 0. $\sum \dfrac{x^n}{n}$ gives the harmonic series at $x = 1$, which diverges, and the alternating harmonic series at $x = -1$, which converges. $\sum\dfrac{x^n}{n^2}$ converges at both ends, since it becomes a p-series with $p = 2$ at $x = 1$ and converges absolutely at $x = -1$.

So the intervals are $(-1, 1)$, $[-1, 1)$ and $[-1, 1]$. **A bracket means the endpoint belongs to the interval and a parenthesis means it does not.** Each endpoint is a numerical series in its own right, and the tests from the last two lessons settle it.

afterFigure.text: The procedure for any power series is therefore in two stages: the ratio test finds $R$ and the open interval, and then each end is checked on its own.

diagram.alt: A number line from minus 2 to 2 with the interval of convergence shaded for three series: the sum of x to the n, the sum of x to the n over n, and the sum of x to the n over n squared. All have radius 1. The first excludes both endpoints, the second includes only minus 1, and the third includes both.
diagram.caption: Same radius, three different intervals: the endpoints have to be tested one at a time.

reveal.text: The ratio tends to $|x|/3$, so the series converges for $|x| < 3$: the factor $n$ in the numerator does not change the radius.

steps.headline: Find the interval of convergence of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x+2)^n}{n\,3^n}$.

workedSteps.text: The ratio tends to $\dfrac{|x + 2|}{3}$, so the radius is 3 and the centre is $-2$.
At $x = 1$ the terms are $\tfrac1n$, the harmonic series, which diverges.
The left-hand end of the interval is $x = -5$, and one more series has to be tested there.

lead.text: Differentiating $1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + \cdots = \dfrac{1}{1-x}$ one term at a time gives $1 + 2x + 3x^2 + \cdots$, and the derivative of $\dfrac1{1-x}$ is $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}$, so $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n\,x^{n-1} = \frac{1}{(1-x)^2}$ for $|x| < 1$. Multiplying by $x$ gives $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n\,x^n = \frac{x}{(1-x)^2}$.

Integrating term by term in the same way gives $x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^3}{3} + \cdots = -\ln(1 - x)$, which is the series $\sum x^n/n$ from 'The endpoints', found as an antiderivative of the geometric series. **The radius stays the same** under both operations, though an endpoint may gain or lose convergence. The formula also settles the series $\sum n/2^n$ from 'Does it settle?', since $x = \tfrac12$ gives $\dfrac{1/2}{(1/2)^2} = 2$.

reveal.text: The sum is 0.75, and $x = \tfrac13$ lies inside the radius $R = 1$, which is what allows the formula to be used.

lessons.orientation: Find the radius and interval of convergence of a power series.
lessons.nextAction: Choose the coefficients so that a power series copies a given function, such as $e^x$ or $\sin x$.

blocks.text: Put a variable into a geometric series and it becomes a function of that variable: $1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + \cdots$ has a sum for some values of $x$ and none for others. At $x = 1.5$ the terms are 1, 1.5, 2.25, 3.375 and so on, which grow without bound, while the function $\dfrac{1}{1-x}$ that the series is meant to equal takes the value $-2$ there, so the series and the function agree only where the series converges.

A sum of this kind, a polynomial that never stops, is called a **power series**. It equals its function only inside an interval around its centre, and the size of that interval tells you where the series can be used in place of the function.

diagram.alt: Graphs of the partial sums 1 plus x plus x squared and so on, of degree 2, 4 or 8, drawn against the function 1 over 1 minus x. Between minus 1 and 1 the polynomial follows the function more closely as the degree rises; beyond x equal to 1 the polynomials climb away and the function does not.
diagram.caption: The polynomial hugs 1/(1 − x) inside |x| < 1 and leaves it outside. Switch the degree.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the radius and interval of convergence of a power series, including the endpoints.
intro.whyItMatters: Power series are polynomials that never stop, and they are how calculators and computers evaluate $e^x$ and $\sin x$.

recap.keyIdea: A power series converges inside an interval of half-width $R$ about its centre, found with the ratio test, and each endpoint is tested on its own.

blocks.text: The ratio test applied to $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$ gives a limit of the form $|x - a|/R$, so the series converges for $|x - a| < R$ and diverges for $|x - a| > R$. At $x = a \pm R$ the test is silent, so each endpoint becomes a numerical series that is tested directly.
Inside the radius a power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term, and the radius is unchanged.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson works backwards: given a function, it chooses the coefficients of the series that copies it.

lessons.title: Functions as polynomials

reveal.text: The value is 1.6458, within 0.003 of $e^{0.5} = 1.6487$. The next screen explains where the coefficients $1, 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac16$ come from.

lead.text: Suppose a polynomial $p(x) = c_0 + c_1x + c_2x^2 + c_3x^3 + \cdots$ is to copy a function $f$ near $x = 0$. At $x = 0$ only $c_0$ survives, so $c_0 = f(0)$. Differentiating gives $p'(x) = c_1 + 2c_2x + 3c_3x^2 + \cdots$ and $p'(0) = c_1$, so $c_1 = f'(0)$. Differentiating again gives $p''(0) = 2c_2$, and a third time $p'''(0) = 6c_3$. Each derivative picks up the factorial of the power, so **$c_n = \dfrac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$**, which is the $n$th derivative divided by $n!$ and not the derivative itself.

For $f(x) = e^x$ every derivative at 0 equals 1, so the coefficients are $\dfrac{1}{n!}$, and $e^x = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2} + \dfrac{x^3}{6} + \cdots$ with terms $\dfrac{x^n}{n!}$. The polynomial that stops at degree $n$ is called the **Taylor polynomial** of degree $n$. A series centred at 0 is also called a **Maclaurin series**.

afterFigure.text: Brook Taylor published his general series in his *Methodus incrementorum* in 1715, and Colin Maclaurin's name is attached to the case at 0 from his 1742 *Treatise of Fluxions*. The method works at any centre $a$, with $f^{(n)}(a)/n!$ and powers of $(x - a)$.

diagram.alt: The curve y equals e to the x, dashed, with its Taylor polynomial about 0 of degree 1, 2, 3 or 4. The polynomials touch the curve at x equal to 0 and fit it more closely over a wider interval as the degree rises.
diagram.caption: Each added term widens the stretch over which the polynomial stays close to e^x. Switch the degree.

reveal.text: The coefficient is $\tfrac16$, since all derivatives of $e^x$ equal 1 at 0 and the factorial $3! = 6$ divides them.
The series begins $1 + 2x + 2x^2 + \cdots$, so $c = 2$, which is also what substituting $2x$ for $x$ in the series for $e^x$ gives: $\dfrac{(2x)^2}{2} = 2x^2$.

lead.text: Differentiating $\sin x$ repeatedly gives $\cos x$, $-\sin x$, $-\cos x$, $\sin x$, and at 0 the values are 1, 0, $-1$, 0 in turn. Only odd powers survive, so $\sin x = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \dfrac{x^5}{5!} - \cdots$. In the same way $\cos x = 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^4}{4!} - \cdots$, with even powers only. Both series converge for every $x$, as the ratio test shows, since the factorials grow faster than any power.

The figure shows the degree 1, 3 and 5 polynomials for sine. Each matches the wave near 0 and drifts away from it farther out, but **a higher degree stays close for longer**. Other functions do not behave so well: $\ln(1 + x) = x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + \dfrac{x^3}{3} - \cdots$ has radius of convergence 1, so its series has no value at $x = 2$ even though $\ln 3$ exists.

afterFigure.text: Two cautions follow. A Taylor polynomial of fixed degree always fits best close to its centre, so adding terms does not make it fit everywhere. And a Taylor series equals its function only where it converges *and* where the error shrinks to 0.

diagram.alt: The sine curve, dashed, with its Taylor polynomial about 0 of degree 1, 3 or 5. Each polynomial matches sine near 0 and drifts away further out, but the larger the degree, the further out it follows the wave.
diagram.caption: Higher-degree polynomials follow the sine curve further from 0 and then leave it. Switch the degree.

workedSteps.text: Write the two terms at $x = 0.5$.
The cube is $0.125$, and dividing by 6 gives $0.0208$, which is the second term.
The cubic term is the amount taken away from the first term.

lead.text: A Taylor polynomial is only useful if its error can be bounded. The **Lagrange error bound** says that, if $|f^{(n+1)}| \le M$ on the interval between the centre and $x$, then $|f(x) - p_n(x)| \le \dfrac{M\,|x|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}$. The bound is the next term of the series, with the derivative replaced by its largest possible size.

For $e^x$ at $x = 0.5$ and degree 3, the fourth derivative is $e^x$, which is at most $e^{0.5} = 1.65$ on the interval, so $M = 2$ is safe. The bound is $\dfrac{2 \times 0.5^4}{4!} = 0.0052$. The actual error is $1.6487 - 1.6458 = 0.0029$, inside the bound, as it must be.

afterFigure.text: With the bound in hand, a polynomial can be *chosen* for a target accuracy: find the first degree at which $M|x|^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ is small enough.

reveal.text: The bound is 0.00026, and the actual error is $0.479426 - 0.479167 = 0.000259$, so here the bound is almost exact.

steps.headline: How many terms of $e^x$ at $x = 1$ guarantee an error below 0.001?

workedSteps.text: On the interval from 0 to 1 the derivatives of $e^x$ are at most $e = 2.72$, so $M = 3$ is safe.
The error of the degree-$n$ polynomial is at most $\dfrac{3}{(n+1)!}$, which must be below 0.001, so $(n+1)!$ must exceed 3000.
The factorials rise as $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$ and $7! = 5040$.

reveal.text: The estimate is 0.5417, about 0.0014 above the true value. The error is smaller than the next term, $\tfrac{1}{720} = 0.0014$, as the bound predicts.

blocks.text: A calculator has no table of values of $e^x$. It has addition, multiplication and division, so to give $e^{0.5}$ it adds up a polynomial: $1 + 0.5 + 0.125 + 0.0208 + 0.0026 + \cdots$, whose terms shrink so fast that five of them already give 1.6484, against the true 1.6487.

The numbers in front of the powers, 1, 1, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac16$ and $\tfrac1{24}$, are chosen so that the polynomial copies the function at a single point, matching its value, its slope, its curvature and every higher rate of change there. A polynomial built this way is called a **Taylor polynomial**.

intro.whyItMatters: Taylor polynomials are how machines evaluate functions, and the error bound says how many terms a given accuracy costs.

recap.keyIdea: The Taylor polynomial of degree $n$ has coefficients $f^{(n)}(0)/n!$ and, when $|f^{(n+1)}| \le M$, an error of at most $M|x|^{n+1}/(n+1)!$.

blocks.text: Matching derivatives at a point gives the coefficients $f^{(n)}(a)/n!$, so that $e^x = \sum x^n/n!$, $\sin x = x - x^3/3! + \cdots$ and $\cos x = 1 - x^2/2! + \cdots$. A fixed polynomial fits best near its centre, and a series equals its function only where it converges and the error tends to 0.
The Lagrange error bound $M|x|^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ then says how many terms a given accuracy needs.

lessons.title: Putting series to work

reveal.text: The three terms give 0.78125, close to 0.7788. Replacing $u$ by $-x^2$ turns the series for $e^u$ into one for $e^{-x^2}$, which the next screen uses.

lead.text: The integral $\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx$ is the area under the bell curve that is central to statistics, and **no combination of the usual functions has $e^{-x^2}$ as its derivative**, so the methods of the earlier lessons cannot find it. Putting $u = -x^2$ in the series for $e^u$ gives $e^{-x^2} = 1 - x^2 + \dfrac{x^4}{2} - \dfrac{x^6}{6} + \cdots$, which holds for every $x$ because the series for $e^u$ has infinite radius.

Integrating each term from 0 to 1 raises the power by one and divides by it: $\int_0^1 x^{2n}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2n+1}$. The integral becomes $1 - \dfrac13 + \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{42} + \dfrac{1}{216} - \cdots$, whose general term is $\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n!\,(2n+1)}$. Integrating term by term is allowed inside the radius of convergence, and here that is the whole real line.

afterFigure.text: This series alternates and its terms shrink fast, so the alternating-series error bound applies: the first term left out limits the error.

steps.headline: How many terms of the series for $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx$ guarantee an error below 0.0001?

workedSteps.text: The series alternates and its terms shrink, so a single term of the series bounds the error. The terms are $\dfrac{1}{n!\,(2n+1)}$.
The terms to keep are all those before $\tfrac1{75600}$.

reveal.text: Only the smallest angle, 0.2 radians, keeps the error near 1 percent. The next screen measures the error across a range of angles.

lead.text: Replacing a function by the first few terms of its series is called **truncation**. For $\sin x = x - \dfrac{x^3}{6} + \cdots$ the first term gives $\sin x \approx x$, and the error is about the size of the next term, $\dfrac{x^3}{6}$. Relative to the sine, that is $\dfrac{x^2}{6}$, which stays below 1 percent only while $x^2 < 0.06$, that is for $x$ up to about 0.24 radians, or 14 degrees.

**The approximation is useful because its error can be stated**, and a statement such as "valid within 1% below 14 degrees" is what separates an approximation from a guess. The same method gives $\dfrac{1}{1+x} \approx 1 - x$ for small $x$, which is the first two terms of a geometric series.

diagram.alt: A curve of the percentage by which the angle x in radians exceeds sin x, against the angle in degrees from 0 to 60. The curve rises slowly: 1 percent at 14 degrees, 4.7 percent at 30 degrees and 20.9 percent at 60 degrees.
diagram.caption: The small-angle error grows faster than the angle: about 1% at 14°, but 21% at 60°.

reveal.text: At 0.5 radians, about 29 degrees, the error is 4.3%, which matches the rise of the curve in the figure.

lead.text: In special relativity a mass $m$ moving at speed $v$ has kinetic energy $mc^2(\gamma - 1)$, with $\gamma = \left(1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^{-1/2}$. For a small ratio $\beta = v/c$ the binomial series gives $\gamma = 1 + \tfrac12\beta^2 + \tfrac38\beta^4 + \cdots$, so the kinetic energy is $mc^2\left(\tfrac12\beta^2 + \tfrac38\beta^4 + \cdots\right) = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac38\dfrac{mv^4}{c^2} + \cdots$.

The first term is the classical formula, and the second is the correction. At $v = 0.1c$ the correction is $\tfrac38\beta^4 = 0.0000375$ against $\tfrac12\beta^2 = 0.005$, only 0.75% of the main term. **The older formula is not wrong, only the first term of a better one**, and the series says exactly how large the error is at any speed.

steps.headline: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \sin(x^2)\,dx$ with the first three terms of its series.

workedSteps.text: Replace $x$ by $x^2$ in $\sin x = x - \dfrac{x^3}{6} + \dfrac{x^5}{120} - \cdots$.
Each of the three terms can be integrated from 0 to 1 by raising its power by one and dividing by the new power, and the results are then added.

reveal.text: The correction is 0.03 of the classical term, so at one fifth of the speed of light the old formula is about 3% low, and at 0.1c it was 0.75%.

blocks.text: The area under the curve $y = e^{-x^2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 1$ is a definite number, and it cannot be found with any antiderivative built from the functions met so far: no combination of powers, exponentials, sines and logarithms has $e^{-x^2}$ as its derivative. The area is nevertheless a number that can be found to any accuracy wanted.

The way to it is to write the function as a power series, which can be integrated term by term inside its radius, so that the integral becomes a sum of simple terms, and the error bound says when to stop.

recap.keyIdea: A power series can be integrated term by term inside its radius, and truncating it gives an approximation whose error is bounded by the next term.

blocks.text: Substituting into a known series and integrating term by term gives $\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx = 1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac1{10} - \cdots = 0.7468$, with the alternating series bound saying when to stop. Truncation gives approximations such as $\sin x \approx x$, whose error is quantified: it stays within 1% only up to about 0.24 radians.
Many classical formulas are the first term of a series, as $\tfrac12mv^2$ is the first term of relativistic kinetic energy.
